claims.text: In a conventional W–Cu composite produced by standard mixing and sintering, copper exists as randomly distributed, isolated particles within a tungsten matrix.
Directional solidification or controlled spark plasma sintering with tailored cooling can promote phase segregation and alignment in W–Cu composites.
The proposed modified processing will form continuous, interconnected copper channels in a tungsten matrix.
The resulting structural mediator is a continuous, percolative copper network embedded within the tungsten matrix.
A contiguous copper phase minimizes thermal boundary resistance across the W–Cu composite.
Reduced thermal boundary resistance facilitates more efficient heat conduction through the composite.
Improved connectivity of the copper phase increases the overall thermal conductivity of the W–Cu composite.
The tungsten matrix provides inherent mechanical durability.
The tungsten matrix provides inherent irradiation resistance.
The modified W–Cu composite will have measurably higher thermal conductivity than an otherwise comparable conventionally processed W–Cu composite.
The modified composite will retain mechanical strength and durability at levels comparable to the conventional W–Cu composite.
The modified composite will retain irradiation resistance at a level comparable to the conventional W–Cu composite.
The predicted effect should hold under fusion-reactor-joint and high-heat-dissipation operating conditions.
Processing-induced defects or microstructural instabilities could compromise performance during prolonged irradiation and thermal cycling.
The long-term stability of the connected copper network under high irradiation flux is uncertain.
